content: 1. The exposure to esomeprazole can more than double, but dose adjustment is generally not required. However, in patients with Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome, who may need higher doses up to 240 mg/day, dose adjustment should be considered. 2. Drugs that induce CYP2C19 and/or CYP3A4 enzymes, such as rifampin, can reduce serum levels of esomeprazole. Omeprazole, the enantiomer of esomeprazole, has been shown to interact with St. John’s Wort, a CYP3A4 inducer. In a crossover study involving 12 healthy male subjects, St. John’s Wort reduced the area under the curve (AUC) and maximum concentration (Cmax) of omeprazole by 37% and 49%, respectively. Concomitant use of St. John’s Wort or rifampin with esomeprazole should be avoided. 3. Drug-induced reductions in gastric acidity can lead to hyperplasia of enterochromaffin-like cells and increased Chromogranin A levels, which may interfere with diagnostic evaluations for neuroendocrine tumors. 4. Co-administration of esomeprazole and tacrolimus may increase serum levels of tacrolimus. 5. The combined use of esomeprazole, clarithromycin, and amoxicillin has been associated with increased plasma levels of esomeprazole and 14-hydroxyclarithromycin. However, clarithromycin, when used with other drugs, can result in serious adverse reactions due to drug interactions. As a result, clarithromycin is contraindicated for co-administration with certain drugs. 6. Case reports, population pharmacokinetic studies, and retrospective analyses suggest that concomitant use of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and methotrexate, particularly at high doses, may elevate and prolong serum levels of methotrexate and/or its metabolite hydroxymethotrexate. However, no formal drug interaction studies between methotrexate and PPIs have been conducted. 7. Esomeprazole is classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies of esomeprazole use in pregnant women. Esomeprazole is the S-isomer of omeprazole. Available epidemiological data do not indicate an increased risk of major congenital malformations or adverse pregnancy outcomes with first-trimester use of omeprazole. 8. Animal reproduction studies with oral esomeprazole magnesium in rats and rabbits at doses approximately 68 times and 42 times the human oral dose of 40 mg (based on body surface area for a 60 kg person) did not show teratogenicity. However, changes in bone morphology were observed in the offspring of rats exposed to doses equal to or greater than approximately 34 times the human oral dose of 40 mg during pregnancy and lactation. Due to these findings, esomeprazole should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. 9. Four epidemiological studies compared the frequency of congenital abnormalities among infants born to women who used omeprazole during pregnancy with those born to women exposed to H2-receptor antagonists or other controls. A population-based retrospective cohort study from the Swedish Medical Birth Registry (1995–1999) reported on 955 infants whose mothers used omeprazole during pregnancy. The rates of malformations, low birth weight, low Apgar scores, and hospitalizations were similar to those in the general population. However, the number of infants with ventricular septal defects and stillbirths was slightly higher in the omeprazole-exposed group than expected. 10. A population-based retrospective cohort study in Denmark (1996–2009) reported on 1,800 live births to mothers who used omeprazole during the first trimester and 837,317 live births to mothers who did not use any proton pump inhibitors. The prevalence of major congenital malformations was 2.9% in the omeprazole-exposed group and 2.6% in the unexposed group. 11. A retrospective cohort study reported on 689 pregnant women exposed to either H2-blockers or omeprazole during the first trimester (134 exposed to omeprazole) and 1,572 pregnant women unexposed to either during the first trimester. The prevalence of major congenital malformations was 4.5% and 3.1%, respectively. 12. A small prospective observational cohort study followed 113 women exposed to omeprazole during pregnancy (89% with first-trimester exposure). Rates of spontaneous and elective abortions, preterm deliveries, gestational age at delivery, and mean birth weight were similar among the groups. 13. Several studies have reported no apparent adverse short-term effects on infants when single-dose oral or intravenous omeprazole was administered to over 200 pregnant women as premedication for cesarean section under general anesthesia. 14. Reproduction studies with esomeprazole magnesium in rats at oral doses up to 280 mg/kg/day (approximately 68 times the human oral dose of 40 mg on a body surface area basis) and in rabbits at oral doses up to 86 mg/kg/day (approximately 41 times the human oral dose of 40 mg on a body surface area basis) revealed no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus due to esomeprazole magnesium.
